newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Rains delay Vietnam coffee crop, prices firmer.
newsitem.headline: Rains delay Vietnam coffee crop, prices firmer.

text.p: Heavy rains have continued to delay harvesting in Vietnam's main coffee-growing region, Dak Lak, and have left many plantations with a problem of excessive moisture in the beans, traders said on Friday.
"The plantations need some sun, and not just one or two days," said one trader. "We need several days of dry weather and then you will see the coffee coming out."

Despite the hold-up, export prices for Vietnamese robusta failed to match this week's strong gains on markets in London and New York. Traders quoted a price of $1,100-$1,120 a tonne, FOB Saigon Port, up from around $1,090 at the end of last week.
Traders in Dak Lak, where about two-thirds of the country's coffee is grown, estimated just 10 percent to 15 percent of the province's 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) crop had been harvested so far.
One trader said some farmers were holding back because of a recent slide in prices, but others said it was the rain rather than prices that was slowing output.
"Farmers are eager to sell coffee because at this time of year they have to buy food and provisions," said another trader.
"It's usually a buyer's market before Tet (the lunar new year). After Tet, much of the crop is usually gone and it's then that people will hold back on remaining stock," he said.
The Tet festival, a time of big consumer spending in Vietnam, is now exactly three months away.
However, he said it may remain a buyers' market even after Tet because a bumper harvest is expected that could leave farmers with above-normal levels of stock.

The Dak Lak-based national Coffee Research Institute told Reuters last month that the current harvest was expected to yield 270,000 tonnes of coffee, a jump of more than 17 percent from last year's 230,000 tonnes.
